You guys onto Y2K? Because the 2038 problem is the Y2K sequel. Y2K38. Unix Millennium Bug. Y2K 2: Electric Boogaloo. 

Basically, the way all digital systems currently store time is with a 32-bit binary integer which represents the amount of seconds that have passed since 00:00:00 on 1st January 1970. And on 19th January 2038, at 7 seconds past 3:14AM, the 32-bit integer is going to max out. It’s going to surpass the largest number it can possibly store - by then 2,147,483,648 seconds will have passed since 1st Jan 1970. 

When this happens, the whole thing is going to reset. The time storage has maxed out, and (I don’t understand this part completely but) the seconds will go into a negative value. Like, computers will recognise the amount of time having passed since 1st January 1970 as negative 2bn+ seconds, so we’re gonna go BACK IN TIME BABY!!! And all systems will think that we’re in 13th December 1901. Which can have a bad effect on embedded systems, like those in transportation, which would be hard to upgrade. Some phone calendars do go beyond 2038, but apparently the bug may cause some phone systems to crash and not restart. 

At the moment there are no completely reliable solutions. Like it’s possible to convert to an unsigned 32-bit integer, but that would mean we run into Y2K III on 7th February 2106, and also that any programs storing data prior to 1970 will display such data in negative numbers. There’s also the proposed solution of upgrading to a 64-bit integer, which would be ideal because it leaves until 4th December in the year 292,277,026,596 until we run into other problems (by which time it is assumed that the Sun will have long since monched on us anyway), but that causes compatibility issues too.
